extracted.intended_audience: aspiring or novice standup comedians and comedy performers learning to recover from bombing
extracted.subtask_description: Practical advice for comedians on how to process, recover from, and learn after a failed standup set (a 'bomb'). Focuses on mindset, immediate behaviors after failure, targeted improvements, and long-term practice strategies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do a lot of work / close the gap
rubrics_metrics.description: Put in high volume of creative work to close the gap between your taste and your current output.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quoting Ira Glass: 'It is only by going through a volume of work that you will close that gap' — put yourself on a deadline so you finish regularly (example: finish one story every week). Repetition and volume are the path from imperfect early work to the level your taste expects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Normalize early failures
rubrics_metrics.description: Accept that early or occasional big failures are normal in a creative career and not a signal to quit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many creatives experience years of work that 'isn’t that good yet.' Recognize bombing as part of the learning curve — most people who do interesting creative work went through this phase. Keeping perspective prevents giving up prematurely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be gracious after bombing
rubrics_metrics.description: Behave kindly and professionally immediately after a bad set so your self-loathing doesn't damage relationships or networking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stay to socialize, thank people who booked or supported you, and avoid letting humiliation 'stink up the room.' Preserving relationships is part of the long game in comedy; a gracious post-show helps maintain opportunities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Find one thing you did well
rubrics_metrics.description: After a bad performance, intentionally identify at least one positive or brave choice you made.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before the memory solidifies into a wholly negative narrative, salvage a small positive takeaway (e.g., 'it was brave to depart from my crafted jokes and try improv'). This frames the failure as part of growth rather than a total disaster.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analyze audience fit / know your audience
rubrics_metrics.description: Reflect on whether you misgauged the crowd — age, sensibilities, and context affect how material lands.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Replay the set and note mismatches (example: the audience was younger and sensitive to certain dating topics). 'Know your audience' is a practical tool to choose or modify material for different rooms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose one focused improvement for next time
rubrics_metrics.description: Pick one concrete, exciting area to work on before your next show rather than trying to overhaul everything.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Set a clear, motivating goal (example: recommit to being precise and tightly scripted while bringing the feeling of improv). Use the momentum from the failure to focus practice and make measurable progress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manage the risk–safety pendulum
rubrics_metrics.description: Understand and accept that your process will swing between safe material and risky experiments; both are necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Risk sometimes produces gems and sometimes produces bombs. Treat this pendulum as a normal part of creative work: alternate honing reliable material and testing risky new ideas in low-stakes rooms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use failures as rehearsal for high-stakes shows
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat bad performances as valuable practice that can help you succeed at important upcoming gigs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After bombing during prep for a big event, the author used that experience to refine and then 'stick to jokes that worked' for the showcase. Intentionally use low-stakes failure to build resilience and tighten material for high-stakes nights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bring a trusted observer / get feedback
rubrics_metrics.description: Have a friend, collaborator, or director attend shows to watch, take notes, and give post-show feedback.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author’s collaborator attended many small shows to provide notes on writing and performance. A consistent external perspective helps identify what to keep, change, or develop.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practice self-care and rituals to cope
rubrics_metrics.description: Use small rituals or comforts to emotionally process failure and reinforce that life continues after a bad set.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Simple acts (example: 'Ice cream. Can help with failure.') can help you recover emotionally. Celebrate both success and failure in small ways to normalize setbacks and maintain morale.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be willing to take risks again
rubrics_metrics.description: After bombing, don’t become risk-averse; incorporate lessons but keep experimenting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author notes that some off-script improvisations later became usable material. Recovering performers should balance learning from mistakes with continued experimentation so growth continues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep the long-term perspective
rubrics_metrics.description: Remember a single bad night isn't career-defining and focus on cumulative progress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame failures as one night among many; prioritize network-building and steady improvement rather than catastrophizing a single performance ('This is just one night. It's not a domino').
